newsitem.title: USA: House passes bill on gas pipeline safety rules.
newsitem.headline: House passes bill on gas pipeline safety rules.

text.p: The House Friday passed a bill to require federal regulators to make more use of risk assessment and cost-benefit studies to set oil and natural gas pipeline safety standards, despite objections from some Democrats that the bill compromised public safety.

The 276-125 vote cleared the legislation to be sent to President Clinton, who has not taken a position on it. The Transportation Department's Office of Pipeline Safety, which regulates pipelines, backed the bill.
The Senate unanimously passed the same bill Thursday.

Backers of the bill said it would let regulators and pipeline companies focus most carefully on pipelines that pose the greatest risk and give pipeline companies leeway to develop plans to improve safety.
But a number of Democrats opposed the bill, saying it created loopholes to allow weaker standards and loaded the regulatory process in the pipeline industry's favor.

"The hard fact is this bill raises more questions than it answers. It puts in place loopholes that raise questions about public safety," said John Dingell, of Michigan, ranking Democrat on the House Commerce Committee.

Rep. Frank Pallone, a New Jersey Democrat who had a natural gas pipeline explosion in his district last year, said Congress should be raising safety standards, not easing them as he said would be done by the bill.

The American Gas Association, which endorsed the bill along with the rest of the natural gas and pipeline industry, in a statement said the bill "would apply a simple and flexible risk assessment and cost-benefit analysis to new pipeline safety regulations."

The bill also authorizes a four-year risk demonstration project which would allow pipeline operators to voluntarily work with the Transportation Department to tailor safety programs for their facilities.

The bill also authorizes funding for the Office of Pipeline Safety through 2000, and caps the industry user fees that fund the office at $27 million for 1997 with three percent increases through 2000.
